turn_text: Your co-chair of the House Hunger Caucus. So prior to this event and after this event, how do you describe to the populace Just how serious hunger is?

Well, we have a hunger problem in this country. Even before the pandemic, tens of millions of our fellow citizens were hungry. They didn't know where the next wheel was going to come from. And hunger defies stereotype. There are people who are homeless, who are hungry, but there are people who are working full-time jobs who are hungry. We have kids who go to school hungry. You know, seeing your citizens are hungry. This is an enormous problem. It has always frustrated me that given the enormity of the problem, given the human impact of the problem, given the financial impact of the problem, that we really never had a plan in this country to solve it. And that's why we had this White House conference. The last time we had a White House conference was in 1969. That was the year we put somebody on the moon. And out of that conference came some really good things, like WIC, the modern day food stamp program, product food labeling, more attention to child nutrition, I mean a whole bunch of stuff. And we began to make progress in the 1970s toward dealing with this issue. And then we started to backslide. And I started, you know, asking for this White House conference during the first term of the Obama administration. And even though they did some good things, they didn't take this issue on as boldly as I would have liked. And Joe Biden became president even before he got sworn in. uh... a a bipartisan group of us uh... myself senator kori booker a democrat for jersey uh... senator brawn of a republican from indiana and jacie allorsky by uh... colleague a republican from indiana who tragically lost her life we all wrote to the president that we need you to do this and he did uh... and so uh... so this is about solving a problem that is huge that uh... has caused enormous suffering on a lot of families, and it is costing us a great deal of money in terms of kids who don't learn in school, lost productivity in the workplace, and avoidable healthcare costs. So we get this right, not only do we improve the well-being and the lives of countless citizens, We also save a whole lot of money in the process.
